title: AI Transformation for Small Businesses: Be the Tortoise, Not the Hare
content:
61% of small businesses now use AI. Only 3.6% run it in a way that changes how the company works. The gap between those numbers is not a technology gap — it is a sequencing gap.

There is a version of AI transformation that fits inside one quarter. You buy a platform, you run a pilot, you announce the results, you move on.

But almost nobody gets through that door. The version that works is slower: six steps, one job per quarter.

The evidence: wide, and very shallow

McKinsey asked 1,719 companies in 97 countries, in the middle of 2026, how they use AI. The answers came in layers, and only the first one is impressive.

Nearly nine in ten (88%) use AI somewhere in the business. 44% say it is now running across the whole company rather than in one team. But ask them to point at money on the bottom line, and only 37% can. That is the same share as the year before, even though more businesses are using AI than ever. And only 6% said the impact was big (5% or more of their profit), also unchanged from the previous year.

Read those together. The first number went up. The money number did not move. More companies bought the thing; the same number of companies can show what it earned them.

Then McKinsey split the results by size, which is the part that should worry anyone running a small business. Among companies under $1 billion in revenue, 22% are running AI agents in production — exactly the same as a year earlier. Large enterprises went from 27% to 40% over those same twelve months. Nobody is standing still, but the big are running while the small are walking.

That flat line is the whole article. You are not behind on tools. The tool was never the missing part.

The OECD’s 2026 survey of small and medium businesses across twelve countries says the same thing with finer detail. 61% use at least one AI application. But 76% of those users are what the OECD calls “AI novices” — off-the-shelf tools, isolated tasks. Only 3.6% qualify as AI Champions: agents and tailored systems deployed across the business. And 44% report minimal or no impact at all.

Then the number I would put on a wall: 2% of firms using AI for isolated tasks report transformational benefits. That rises to 23% when AI is deployed across the enterprise. Same technology. Different arrangement. Eleven times the result.

Everyone says it works. Almost nobody can show you where.

None of this means waiting for a perfect plan. It means moving at your own pace, on your own spectrum: one job in, one job done, then the next.

Why the hare loses

I have watched small companies make the same four mistakes, in roughly this order. They buy a tool before choosing a process, because the purchase feels like progress. They automate a broken process and get the same mess, faster, with less judgement in the loop. They audit all the data at once and turn one workflow into a six-month project that ships nothing. And they announce before measuring, which makes every later result an opinion.

The last one is epidemic. The 2026 QuickBooks study surveyed 34,000 small businesses: 41% said AI had increased their revenue. Asked how they knew, more than half described “a general feeling.”

Step 1 — Pick one job, and write down the baseline

Every AI agent sits on three rungs below it — data, connectors, workflows — and each rung stays useful without the rung above it. That is the design test.

Most SMEs try to enter at the top. The ladder does not fail. The entry point does. So not a department, not a strategy: one repeating job, with a name.

The good first jobs share a profile: repeats weekly, has a named owner today, the data it needs is digital and one person can reach it, a human can check the output in two minutes, and getting it wrong is annoying rather than catastrophic. Quoting. Lead follow-up. Support triage. Invoice matching. Report assembly. The unglamorous middle of your business.

Before you build anything, write down four numbers: hours per week, volume per month, rework rate, turnaround time. That paragraph is your baseline, and your only defence against a vendor’s demo and your own enthusiasm.

Step 2 — Fix the data that job touches, and nothing else

Data readiness is a property of a process, not a company — your quoting process can be ready while your reporting is a disaster, and a business-wide “data score” averages the two into a number that describes neither.

So scope it. List every record your chosen job touches, then run three checks on ten random samples:

  1. Completeness. Are the fields the job needs populated, or is half the sample blank?
  2. Duplicates. Search for a customer you know appears twice. Does the system treat them as one entity or three?
  3. Readability. Can a machine read these records directly, or does someone open, copy, paste and convert first?

That is the whole audit. An hour, maybe two. The bar is reachability, not perfection: if an external analyst could assemble the dataset on a Wednesday afternoon, you have enough to ship. If they would need a month, the data is the project. No warehouse required — an export from one system, sometimes joined to a second, is enough.

Step 3 — Connect the systems before you add intelligence

Four failure modes appear almost every time an AI layer sits on top of systems that never agreed with each other:

  • Duplicate entities. One customer, three IDs across CRM, ERP and accounting. The agent picks one, never knowing it chose.
  • Timing gaps. Sales marked the deal won; finance has not invoiced. Ask twice, get two answers.
  • Conflicting definitions. “Revenue” means deal value in the CRM and recognised revenue in accounting. A summary mixing them is confidently wrong.
  • No safe write path. An agent creating orders without duplicate protection turns one retry into two orders.

So do the boring work first. Pick one system of record per entity, write the decision down, and add idempotency keys and an error queue — networks drop, and systems go down for maintenance. Only then give the AI hands: read-only first (answer questions, cite the source records), then suggest (draft the quote, propose the merge), then act with human approval wherever money or compliance is involved.

This is the same lesson as my AI agent reading my AWS credentials: the incident is never the model being clever. It is the model having a write path it should not have had. In July 2025, a coding agent with direct production access deleted a live database during an explicit code freeze. If you cannot list every path that writes into your system of record today, you are not ready to add one — however good the data looks.

Step 4 — Build it modular, because the ground is moving

In 2026 the ground moved a lot. Anthropic retired Claude Sonnet 4 and Opus 4 in June, then Opus 4.1 in August; OpenAI shut down its entire Assistants API that same summer. None of it was a surprise — every provider published dates in advance.

The problem was on the builder’s side. Teams that made the model the foundation of their system rebuilt the building when the foundation moved. Teams that treated the model as replaceable compute behind an interface changed a line of configuration. If your model ID is hard-coded in twelve places, that retirement notice is a migration project; if it lives in one config file, it is an afternoon.

Four properties make a swap routine instead of a project:

  1. One interface. Application code calls your own function, never a provider SDK. Provider logic lives in one adapter module.
  2. Configuration selects the model. Which model serves which task is data, changeable without a release.
  3. Data you control. Prompts in version control, history and documents in your own database, original text kept so an index can be rebuilt.
  4. An evaluation set. Twenty real cases with known right answers. Without it, a swap is a guess and fear keeps you on the old model.

Here is what most “just use a gateway” advice skips: code portability is cheap, behavioural portability is not. A prompt tuned to one model’s quirks does not transfer — which is why the evaluation set matters more than the abstraction layer. Sixty days of retirement notice is plenty for a team with one, and almost nothing for a team without.

The trade-offs are real: you lag behind provider features, you get the common denominator, and a gateway is one more component to run. Keep the layer thin, with a documented escape hatch.

Step 5 — Review every output, and keep the manual path alive

Treat the AI as a new member of the organisation. New members do not get production access on day one, their work gets checked, and someone else can do the job if they are unavailable. In practice: a confidence threshold, an exception queue, a named reviewer, and nothing leaves the building without a human signature.

Then write the fallback. One page: how a person does this job by hand, in twenty minutes, when the tool is down, degraded, or retired. That is not paranoia. In one week this month, Chase, Wells Fargo, Truist and United Airlines all had outages, and Microsoft traced a global email outage to a defect from a July fix.

I keep a Telegram bridge to my local coding agent for exactly this reason — not to make the agent impressive, but so I can see what it is doing and take the wheel. The same instinct applies to a quoting agent: the ability to take over is a feature.

Step 6 — Measure, decide, then pick job number two

Give each job a 90-day cycle. Long enough to reach production, short enough to stop.

At day 90, choose against your baseline: keep, change scope, or stop. Keeping something that saves two hours a week is fine. Killing something that saves none is better. Then do it again — one job per cycle, four a year, twenty over five years, each resting on the data and connectors the previous one left behind.

Who to hire, and how to spot the wrong one

The person you want is not an IT generalist, and I say that without malice. Keeping systems running is administration: accounts, licences, backups, the printer. Building systems is engineering: interfaces, data models, integrations, evaluation, failure modes. They are different jobs that overlap on paper and rarely in practice.

You probably do not need that person full time. A fractional CTO or an independent builder on a retainer is the right shape for most small companies — senior enough to sequence the work, hands-on enough to ship it. This is the work I do through Great Wall Connect, so weigh that accordingly.

Where to look. Three sources beat everything else:

  • Other owners with a system that is actually running. Not someone who “did an AI project” — someone whose quoting or reporting works differently now, who can show you the screen.
  • People who build in public. Open-source repositories, technical writing with working demos, talks with code in them. A portfolio you can read beats one you are shown.
  • One person who does the work. For an SME, a builder who ships beats an agency that subcontracts, because nobody in the chain owns the outcome.

What to ask. Four questions separate builders from talkers:

  1. Show me something you built that is still running.
  2. What would you not automate first, and why?
  3. What happens when the model you chose gets retired?
  4. Who owns this after you leave, and where is the documentation?

Red flags. They propose a platform before agreeing on a process. They earn commission on the tool they recommend. The first deliverable is a strategy deck. There is no measurement plan, or the plan is “we’ll track adoption”. The contract is a fixed-price “transformation programme” rather than a 90-day proof you can stop.

Structure the engagement so failure stays cheap: 90 days to prove one job, then a retainer to do the next. Pay for a working system, not hours. Insist every account, repository and credential lives in your name from day one, because the day it does not is the day you have a new hostage.

A consultant who hands you a roadmap and leaves has sold you the hare’s plan. You want the person who stays for the boring middle.

The marathon part

“Most people overestimate what they can do in one year and underestimate what they can do in ten years.”

Bill Gates said it about software. It is more true about AI Transformation.

One year at a sprint produces a subscription stack, a slide, and a team that quietly went back to the spreadsheet. Ten years at a walk — one job per quarter, modular enough to survive every retirement, measured honestly — produces a company competitors cannot copy in a quarter, because there is nothing to copy.

AI will not replace your people. But companies that use AI will replace companies that do not.

Not next quarter, and probably not next year. In five years, or ten, with the confidence of arithmetic. And the ones that get replaced will not be the ones that chose the wrong model. They will be the ones that never moved.

So move. Slowly, deliberately, in one direction. Be the tortoise.
